entries.question: Do evildoers prosper?
entries.summary: Job 12:6 says the tents of robbers prosper and those who provoke God are secure. Psalm 73:3-7, 12 describes the prosperity of the wicked at length — they are not in trouble, they wear pride as a necklace, they increase in riches. Jeremiah 12:1 asks why the way of the wicked prospers. Against this, Psalm 34:21 says evil shall slay the wicked and those who hate the righteous shall be desolate. The biblical wisdom and poetic tradition contains both empirical observations that evil prospers and theological assertions that it does not.
entries.commentary:
This is the same theological tension that runs through the previous entry on whether God destroys the righteous along with the wicked, but with a different rhetorical framing. The question of whether evildoers prosper is the empirical question; the question of whether they should is the theological one. The Hebrew Bible repeatedly notices that the empirical answer is yes — Job, Psalm 73, and Jeremiah 12 all describe the prosperity of the wicked as an observable fact that creates a theological problem for those who hold to the doctrine of strict retribution. Psalm 34:21 represents the doctrinal counter-claim that the empirical observation is wrong or temporary.

The apologetic harmonization here is usually a long-term-versus-short-term distinction. The wicked prosper now, but they will be desolate eventually — whether in this life through eventual divine judgment or in the next life through final judgment. This is the position taken by Kidner in his Tyndale Old Testament Commentary on Psalms and by most evangelical readers of the wisdom literature. On this reading, Job 12, Psalm 73, and Jeremiah 12 are describing temporary prosperity, while Psalm 34:21 is describing ultimate outcome. The two are compatible because they operate on different time horizons.

The harmonization has force where the texts themselves signal the long-term framing. Psalm 73 explicitly resolves its complaint by retreating to the sanctuary and recognizing the final destruction of the wicked (Psalm 73:17-20), which fits the long-term reading. The problem is that not all the texts in question allow this resolution. Job 12:6 is a flat empirical claim with no eschatological corrective in context — Job is describing the way the world actually works, and the whole book of Job refuses to resolve the problem of suffering by appeal to an afterlife (which Israelite theology of this period did not have in any developed form). Jeremiah 12:1 is a complaint addressed to God demanding an explanation, and the answer Jeremiah gets (Jeremiah 12:5) is essentially that things are going to get worse, not that the wicked will be punished.

The critical conclusion is that the Hebrew Bible preserves competing views on this question because Israelite religion went through a long, painful process of confronting the empirical failure of strict retribution and developing alternative theological frameworks to cope with it. Some texts hold to retribution. Other texts give it up and admit the wicked prosper. Still others develop a long-term framework that defers the resolution to the end of life or to the eschaton. All three frameworks coexist in the canon. The apologetic harmonization works for some texts and fails for others, which is what we would expect from a canon that preserves genuinely different theological responses to the same problem. The honest read is theological pluralism, not a single consistent doctrine.

entries.question: Do the wicked live long?
entries.books_in_tension: Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Jeremiah, Nahum
entries.summary: Job 21:7 stares straight at the problem of evil and admits that the wicked do, in fact, live long and grow mighty. Psalm 55:23, Proverbs 10:27, Proverbs 24:20, Ecclesiastes 8:13, Jeremiah 23:19, and Nahum 1:3 all insist on the opposite — the wicked get their days cut short and their lamp snuffed out. The contradiction is between observed reality (Job, and arguably Ecclesiastes when read whole) and the moralizing slogans of the deuteronomistic and sapiential traditions.
entries.commentary:
This is one of those contradictions where the Hebrew Bible is openly arguing with itself in plain sight. Proverbs runs on a retribution principle — righteousness lengthens days, wickedness shortens them — and so do large chunks of Deuteronomy and the prophets. Job 21 is a frontal assault on that whole framework. Job's complaint is not abstract theodicy; it is the empirical observation that wicked people live long, wealthy, well-fed lives and die peacefully in bed. Ecclesiastes oscillates: 8:13 repeats the Proverbs line, but 7:15 and 8:14 grant that the righteous perish in their righteousness while the wicked prolong their life. Qohelet contradicts himself within two adjacent chapters; the canon contradicts itself across genres.

The standard apologist move, found in Gleason Archer's Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties and in Walter Kaiser's Hard Sayings of the Bible, is to claim these are different literary modes — Proverbs offers general principles, Job offers exceptions, the prophets give long-term eschatological outcomes. That is of course a subjective reading. It also concedes the point: if the Proverbs claims are merely general tendencies, then they are not actually true as stated, and Job is not contradicting them but exposing them. Carol Newsom's Anchor Bible commentary on Job treats the book as a deliberate destabilization of the wisdom tradition; the contradiction is the literary engine, not an accident.

The critical-scholarship consensus, going back to Crenshaw and Murphy, is that Israelite wisdom literature contains an internal debate between act-consequence retribution (Proverbs) and protest theology (Job, parts of Qohelet, Psalm 73). Trying to harmonize Job 21:7 with Proverbs 10:27 by appealing to literary genre does not make the contradiction disappear — it just relocates it. Either the wicked actually live shorter lives (empirically false, as Job notes) or the proverbial claim is a moralizing fiction.

Verdict: the contradiction is real, it is intra-canonical, and it is the whole point of Job. Take your pick — but you cannot have both at face value.

entries.question: Who brought evil on Job?
entries.summary: Job 2:7 says Satan smote Job with the boils. Job 42:11 — the narrator, in the prose epilogue — attributes "all the evil that the LORD had brought upon him" to Yahweh directly. The book itself can't keep the story straight: in the prologue Yahweh outsources the suffering, in the epilogue Yahweh owns it.
entries.commentary:
This is not a trivial harmonization problem. The Hebrew word at Job 42:11 is ra'ah, evil/calamity, and the verb is the H-stem of bo' — "the evil that Yahweh caused to come upon him." The narrator, telling the audience what happened, attributes the disaster directly to Yahweh. Meanwhile in 1:6-12 and 2:1-7 Yahweh tells ha-satan — "the satan," which in the Hebrew is a definite article + common noun meaning "the adversary," not a proper name — that he can strike Job. Even there, Yahweh permits, authorizes, and effectively orders the disaster. The satan in Job is not yet the Satan of later Christian demonology; he is a member of the divine council functioning as a kind of prosecutor.

The standard apologist move (Archer, Geisler) is to say Yahweh allowed it while Satan caused it, so both verses are true under a doctrine of secondary causation. That works only if you import a much later theology of agency back into the text. The Joban author has no such category. The book's own answer, given in the divine speeches of chapters 38-41 and in 42:11, is that Yahweh did this. The whole point of the dialogues is Job's complaint against God, not against an adversary. Job never blames the satan. He cannot — he doesn't know about the heavenly wager. Carol Newsom and David Clines both note that the prose frame and the poetic dialogues operate with different theological vocabularies; the contradiction is partly between the folk-tale prologue and the later poetic core.

The critical position, articulated by Marvin Pope in the Anchor Bible volume and refined by Newsom, is that ha-satan in Job is a divine-council functionary, not the cosmic evil agent of 1 Enoch or the New Testament. The contradiction at 42:11 is the narrator letting the original monotheistic theology bleed through: Yahweh is the source of weal and woe, exactly as Isaiah 45:7 says outright. Trying to harmonize "Satan did it" with "Yahweh did it" by invoking permission-versus-causation is a much later theological grid pasted onto an earlier text that didn't need it.

Verdict: the book of Job itself contains the contradiction. The narrator at 42:11 sides with the older, harder theology — Yahweh did this — and the apologetic harmonization works only by anachronism.

entries.question: Is it good to be foolish?
entries.summary: Paul in 1 Corinthians 1:21, 3:18, and 4:10 actively recommends becoming a fool — God saves through the foolishness of preaching, and Paul calls himself and his colleagues "fools for Christ." Psalm 5:5 says the foolish cannot stand before God, and Ephesians 5:15 (a disputed-Pauline letter) tells believers not to walk as fools but as wise. The two halves of the canon, and arguably the two halves of the Pauline corpus, are pulling in opposite directions on whether foolishness is laudable or condemned.
entries.commentary:
The harmonization here is partly genuine and partly papered-over. Paul in 1 Corinthians is doing rhetorical inversion — the Greek word mōria (foolishness) is reclaimed as a polemical badge against the wisdom (sophia) the Corinthian elites are chasing. Apologists like D. A. Carson and Anthony Thiselton point out, correctly, that Paul is not saying actual cognitive foolishness is virtuous; he is saying the cross looks foolish to Greco-Roman wisdom culture, and that is a feature, not a bug. Fine. That is what 1 Corinthians 1-4 is doing.

But Psalm 5:5 uses holelim (boasters, the arrogantly foolish), not the same conceptual category as Pauline mōria. And Ephesians 5:15 uses asophos — literally "unwise" — and the author is telling Christians to be sophoi, exactly what Paul in 1 Corinthians is mocking. Most critical scholars — Ernest Best in the ICC and Margaret MacDonald in the Sacra Pagina commentary among them — treat Ephesians as deutero-Pauline, written by a later admirer who had absorbed Pauline themes but did not have Paul's polemical context against Corinthian wisdom-elitism. So the tension here is partly an authentic Paul versus pseudo-Paul issue: the historical Paul weaponizes "foolishness," while the post-Pauline tradition retreats to conventional Hellenistic moralism.

The apologist response — "different kinds of foolishness, different rhetorical contexts" — is technically correct on the lexical question but glosses over what is actually happening. The canon is preserving two distinct theological currents: Paul's apocalyptic inversion of worldly status markers, and the later church's accommodation to Greco-Roman virtue ethics. Both currents are visible in the New Testament; they sit uneasily next to the Wisdom literature of the Hebrew Bible, which is unambiguously pro-wisdom. Trying to read 1 Corinthians 3:18 ("become a fool that you may be wise") and Proverbs 1:7 ("fools despise wisdom") as saying the same thing in different words requires you to ignore what Paul is actually arguing.

Verdict: this is a soft contradiction in surface vocabulary and a real contradiction in underlying theology — apocalyptic Paul versus moralizing wisdom tradition.

entries.question: Where does God dwell?
entries.summary: Psalm 9:11, 76:2, 132:13-14, and Joel 3:17, 21 lock Yahweh's residence into Mount Zion — chosen, desired, permanent. Psalm 123:1 and Ecclesiastes 5:2 just as flatly locate God in heaven, with the earth (including Zion) explicitly down here and God up there. The Hebrew Bible cannot pick a divine zip code.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the cleaner specimens of the theological evolution that critical scholars have been mapping for 150 years. The Zion-residence theology in Psalms 76 and 132 belongs to what Frank Moore Cross and Jon Levenson identified as the Zion tradition — a royal-priestly ideology centered on the Jerusalem temple, in which Yahweh literally dwells on the holy mountain. This is not metaphor in those texts; the language of mōshāb (dwelling place) and m'nukhah (resting place) in Psalm 132:13-14 is concrete real-estate vocabulary, drawn from Canaanite divine-mountain motifs that Mark Smith has tracked in detail.

Then you have the heaven-dwelling tradition, which gets louder in exilic and post-exilic texts — Deuteronomistic theology in particular pushes Yahweh's residence into the heavens and keeps only Yahweh's "name" in the Jerusalem temple (Deuteronomy 12:5, 1 Kings 8:27-30 — "will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you"). Ecclesiastes 5:2 is late Second Temple Wisdom material that simply assumes the heavenly-residence model. Psalm 123:1 fits this pattern.

The apologist response (Walton, Hamilton, the IVP commentary) is to say God dwells in heaven essentially but localizes presence at Zion sacramentally. That theological move is real — you can find it in 1 Kings 8 — but it is itself a harmonization, attempted from within the text, between two originally distinct theologies. Israel Knohl, Mark Smith, and Stephen Geller have all shown that the Priestly source insists on Yahweh's tabernacle-dwelling, the Deuteronomist insists on Yahweh's heavenly throne with only the divine name at the sanctuary, and the Psalms preserve fragments of both — sometimes in the same psalm. The contradiction isn't between two sloppy authors; it is between two competing schools of Israelite religion that the canon never fully merged.

Verdict: real contradiction, well-documented in source-critical scholarship, and the harmonization ("essentially heaven, sacramentally Zion") is itself a post-hoc theological synthesis. The two strands disagree on a basic ontological question.

entries.question: Is every word of God pure?
entries.books_in_tension: 2 Kings, Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Habakkuk, Malachi
entries.summary: Psalm 12:6, 119:140, and Proverbs 30:5 claim every word of Yahweh is pure, refined like silver. The SAB then lines up 2 Kings 18:27 / Isaiah 36:12 (eating dung and drinking piss), Ezekiel 23:20 (flesh of asses, issue of horses), Habakkuk 2:16 (foreskin uncovered), and Malachi 2:3 (dung on faces) as examples of scriptural language that does not fit any sane definition of "pure." The contradiction here depends on what "pure" is doing in the wisdom claim.
entries.commentary:
This one needs more lexical care than the SAB framing gives it. The Hebrew of Psalm 12:7 uses tehorot (from tahor, ritually pure), and Proverbs 30:5 uses tseruphah (from tsaraph, refined as silver in a furnace) — both belong to the same semantic field of purity/refinement. The claim there is about the truthfulness and reliability of Yahweh's revelation, not about whether the Bible avoids vulgar vocabulary. The apologist response (Archer, Geisler, the standard inerrancy literature) is correct that "pure" does not mean "PG-rated." Hebrew prophetic literature uses brutally graphic language for theological purposes — Ezekiel 23 is the most notorious example, where Oholah and Oholibah's promiscuity is described in language that would not pass a censor today.

That said, the underlying tension the SAB is pointing at is real, just located differently than its prooftexts suggest. If "every word of God is pure" is a doctrine of verbal inerrancy and divine refinement, then critical scholarship has plenty of harder counter-evidence than the dung-and-piss verses: textual variants between MT and LXX show God's "pure words" coming down to us in multiple competing versions (Eugene Ulrich, Emanuel Tov on textual pluriformity); the documentary sources of the Pentateuch contradict each other on basic narrative facts; the LXX of Jeremiah is one-eighth shorter than the MT. Which "pure word" do you mean? The phrase becomes incoherent under historical scrutiny.

In 2 Kings 18:27 and Isaiah 36:12 specifically, the Masoretes themselves were embarrassed enough by the language to substitute a Qere reading — they euphemized "piss" and "dung" in the margins. The text knows it is rough. So apologists are right that the SAB's prooftexts don't show what they claim; critical scholars are right that the actual problem with "every word of God is pure" is textual transmission and source-critical incoherence, not vulgar vocabulary. The contradiction is real, but the SAB has picked weak ammunition.

entries.question: Is it OK to call someone a fool?
entries.summary: Psalm 14:1 and 53:1 — same text, double-edited — open with "the fool has said in his heart, there is no God." Calling someone a fool there is fine; the Psalmist does it freely. Matthew 5:22 has Jesus declare that whoever says "You fool" (rhaka, mōre) is liable to the fire of Gehenna. The contradiction is internal to the canon and stings sharper because Jesus himself calls people fools in Matthew 23:17 and Luke 11:40.
entries.commentary:
The Greek in Matthew 5:22 is mōre — vocative of mōros, root of "moron." Jesus prohibits its use under threat of hellfire. Then eighteen chapters later in Matthew 23:17 he addresses the Pharisees as "mōroi kai typhloi" — fools and blind. Same word. Same speaker. Same gospel. Luke 11:40 has him calling the Pharisees aphrones, a near-synonym. This is not a translation artifact; the Greek is unambiguous and Davies and Allison's ICC commentary on Matthew flags the tension directly.

The apologist harmonization (Blomberg, Carson, France) usually takes one of three routes. First, that mōre in 5:22 is a particular kind of contemptuous insult (sometimes argued to be Aramaic moreh, "rebel," rather than Greek mōros) and Jesus is condemning hateful contempt rather than the word itself. Second, that the Sermon on the Mount is hyperbolic moral teaching not meant as juridical rule. Third, that Jesus, being divine, has authority to use the word in ways humans cannot. None of these survives scrutiny. The Aramaic-moreh argument is a textual-criticism guess with no manuscript support and is rejected by Davies and Allison and by Ulrich Luz. The hyperbole argument concedes that Matthew 5:22 doesn't actually mean what it says. The divine-authority argument is the apologist playbook's last resort and would let any inconsistency off the hook.

The critical position, articulated by Hans Dieter Betz in his Hermeneia commentary on the Sermon on the Mount and by Luz in his three-volume Matthew, is that Matthew 5:22 belongs to the antitheses where Jesus intensifies Torah requirements rhetorically, while Matthew 23 reflects later anti-Pharisaic polemic from the Matthean community after the Jewish-Christian split. The two passages were composed in different rhetorical contexts and the redactor of Matthew did not smooth them. Add the Psalms freely using "fool" as a theological category, and you have a canon that prohibits, uses, and rewards the same insult.

Verdict: real contradiction within a single gospel. The harmonizations require either rewriting the Greek, downgrading the Sermon on the Mount to hyperbole, or pleading divine exception. Take your pick.

entries.question: Does anyone ever do anything good?
entries.books_in_tension: Psalms, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, John, Romans, 2 Corinthians, 3 John
entries.summary: Psalm 14:3, Psalm 53:3, and Paul quoting them at Romans 3:12 say absolutely no one does good — not one. Ecclesiastes 7:20 and Isaiah 64:6 ("all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags") double down. Then John 5:29 talks about "those who have done good" rising to the resurrection of life, 2 Corinthians 5:10 has Christ judging each according to what he did "whether good or bad," and 3 John 11 distinguishes "he who does good" from "he who does evil." The New Testament cannot decide if doing good is impossible or required.
entries.commentary:
This contradiction lives at the heart of Pauline theology versus the rest of the New Testament. Paul in Romans 3 is constructing his total-depravity argument to set up justification by faith — he chains together Psalm 14, Isaiah 59, and other texts to demonstrate that no human achieves righteousness apart from Christ. Joseph Fitzmyer's Anchor Yale commentary on Romans treats 3:10-18 as a Pauline florilegium, a rhetorical catena, not a metaphysical claim that human beings literally cannot perform any beneficial action. That is a real exegetical point.

The apologist harmonization (Carson, Schreiner, Moo) is to distinguish between "doing good" in the absolute soteriological sense — meriting salvation, satisfying God's holiness — and "doing good" in the ordinary moral sense. Paul means no one is righteous before God by works; the other texts mean Christians or even non-Christians can perform morally good actions. This is a real distinction in systematic theology, and Augustinian/Reformed traditions have made it for centuries.

But the texts themselves don't always cooperate. Matthew 19:17 has Jesus saying "if you want to enter into life, keep the commandments" — keeping commandments is something humans can do. John 5:29 explicitly divides people into doers of good and doers of evil, with eschatological consequences. Romans 2:6-13, which Paul writes one chapter before his "none is righteous" catena, says God will render to each according to his works and "the doers of the law will be justified." Paul contradicts himself within Romans, and the synoptic-Johannine tradition operates with a different anthropology than Pauline total depravity. James Dunn, Krister Stendahl, and E. P. Sanders have all argued that the traditional Reformation reading of Paul as teaching universal moral incapacity is itself a post-Augustinian theological imposition that the texts do not require.

Verdict: the contradiction is real, but it is partly produced by reading Paul through Augustinian glasses. The actual New Testament data is messier — Paul, Jesus, John, and James are each working with somewhat different anthropologies. The harmonization works if you collapse all those voices into Pauline-Reformation soteriology, which is exactly the move critical scholarship has been challenging since Sanders.

entries.question: Does God listen to and answer prayers?
entries.summary: Proverbs 2:3-5, Proverbs 8:17, and Matthew 7:8 / Luke 11:9-10 promise that anyone who seeks God will find him — ask and receive, knock and the door opens. Psalm 18:41, Proverbs 1:28, Lamentations 3:8 and 3:44, and Luke 13:24 directly contradict this: God refuses to answer, shuts out prayer, hides behind a cloud, and tells seekers they will not be able to enter. The contradiction is canonical, intra-testamental, and even intra-Proverbial.
entries.commentary:
This is unusually clean because the same book — Proverbs — gives both answers. Proverbs 8:17 has Wisdom say "those who seek me find me," while Proverbs 1:28 has Wisdom say "then they shall call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me diligently but they shall not find me." The author of Proverbs is constructing a moralized framework where the timing of one's seeking determines the result. Fine — that is a real harmonization within the wisdom tradition, and Michael V. Fox notes it in the Anchor Yale volume.

But Matthew 7:7-8 and Luke 11:9-10 have Jesus issuing an unqualified promise: pas gar ho aitōn lambanei — "for everyone who asks receives." No timing condition. Luke 13:24, two chapters later, has the same Jesus warning that many will seek to enter and not be able. The Lamentations 3 verses are even worse for the harmonization, because they come from someone (the speaker) who is desperately seeking and being shut out. Lamentations 3:8 — "even when I call and cry for help, he shuts out my prayer" — is not a wisdom warning about ill-timed prayer; it is a description of divine silence in the face of legitimate suffering. Adele Berlin's commentary in the Old Testament Library treats this as theodicy protest, parallel to Job's complaints.

The apologist response (Wenham, Carson, Blomberg on Matthew) is the standard "qualified promises" move: the Matthean promise to seekers assumes good-faith repentance, the Lukan warning addresses last-minute opportunists, the Lamentations cry reflects a temporary divine hiddenness. That is a coherent theological synthesis, but it is doing exactly what every harmonization does — adding conditions the text itself does not specify. If Jesus had said "everyone who asks in repentance and persistence and good timing receives," we wouldn't be having this conversation. He didn't say that. The harmonization smuggles in qualifiers.

Verdict: contradiction is real; the harmonization works only by importing conditions the texts omit. The lived-experience verses (Lamentations, Psalm 18:41) are the strongest evidence that the unqualified promise of Matthew 7:8 was already known to be empirically false within the biblical corpus itself.

entries.question: Is the law of God perfect?
entries.summary: Psalm 19:7 says the Torah of Yahweh is perfect (temimah), converting the soul. Hebrews 8:6-7 says if the first covenant had been faultless (amemptos), no place would have been sought for a second — and the author of Hebrews is arguing that exactly this second, better covenant was needed because the first was deficient. Old Testament confidence in the law, meet New Testament supersessionism.
entries.commentary:
The contradiction is precisely between Second Temple Jewish covenant theology and the Christian replacement theology of Hebrews. The Hebrew word in Psalm 19:7 is temimah — complete, whole, unblemished. The Greek of Hebrews 8:7 says ei gar he prōtē ekeinē ēn amemptos — "for if that first one had been faultless." Hebrews is straightforwardly arguing that the first covenant was faulty and needed replacing. Harold Attridge's Hermeneia commentary on Hebrews and Craig Koester's Anchor Yale volume both treat this as classic Christian supersessionist argumentation built on a midrashic reading of Jeremiah 31:31-34.

The apologist response (Lane, Bruce, Ellingworth) is to distinguish between the law itself being perfect as a revelation of God's will (Psalm 19) and the Mosaic covenant administration being inadequate as a means of salvation (Hebrews 8). On this reading, the Torah is morally perfect; the covenantal arrangement was always meant as preparatory. This is the standard Reformed and dispensationalist solution and it has internal coherence. Hebrews itself doesn't quite say the law is morally defective — it says the covenant was incomplete and pointed forward to Christ.

But Hebrews 7:18-19 ("the former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness" — atheteō and astheneia) and 10:1 ("the law has only a shadow of the good things to come, not the true form") push much harder than the apologetic gloss admits. The author of Hebrews is not just saying the administration was provisional; he is calling the commandment itself weak and useless. That is a frontal collision with Psalm 19:7's temimah. James Dunn and Pamela Eisenbaum have both noted that Hebrews represents the most aggressive supersessionist voice in the New Testament canon, and that its theology of the law cannot be smoothly harmonized with Second Temple Jewish (or Pauline) understandings of Torah.

Verdict: real contradiction. Hebrews 8:6-7 is not merely saying the administration was preparatory; it is grading the first covenant as faulty. The Psalmist would not have agreed. The apologetic harmonization works only by softening Hebrews' language past what the Greek will bear.

entries.question: Is wealth a sign of righteousness or of wickedness?
entries.summary: Psalm 37:25, Psalm 112:1-3, Proverbs 13:22, and Proverbs 15:6 all treat wealth as a marker of divine favor — the righteous never beg, their houses fill with treasure, and the sinner's wealth ends up with the just. Matthew 19:23-24, Luke 6:24, and James 5:1 reverse the polarity completely: rich men can barely enter the kingdom of heaven, the rich have already received their consolation, and they should weep and howl for the miseries coming on them. The Hebrew Bible's retribution-prosperity theology and the synoptic/Jacobean apocalyptic theology are working from opposite playbooks.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest theological contradictions in the canon and critical scholarship has been mapping it for over a century. The Deuteronomistic and sapiential traditions operate on what Klaus Koch and others called the act-consequence connection (Tun-Ergehen-Zusammenhang): righteousness produces prosperity, wickedness produces poverty. Proverbs runs on this principle as its default theology. Psalm 112:1-3 is its purest crystallization — fear the Lord, get wealth.

The synoptic tradition, especially Luke, reverses this. Luke 6:24 (the woes following the beatitudes) and the Magnificat in Luke 1:51-53 ("he has sent the rich away empty") encode what scholars from Joachim Jeremias to Halvor Moxnes have called Lukan reversal theology — the eschatological inversion of social position. Matthew 19:24 (the camel and the needle) is one of the strongest anti-wealth sayings in the gospels and is widely judged authentic to Jesus by virtually all critical reconstructions including the Jesus Seminar database. James 5:1-6 stands in the prophetic tradition of Amos and Micah denouncing the rich as oppressors, full stop.

The apologist harmonization (Blomberg's Neither Poverty nor Riches is the most sustained version) tries to thread the needle: wealth is a blessing when received righteously and used generously, a danger when it becomes idolatrous or oppressive. That is a pastoral synthesis with real exegetical support from passages like 1 Timothy 6:17-19 ("command those who are rich in this world... to be rich in good works"). The problem is that the synthesis is itself a third position invented to harmonize the first two. Proverbs is not saying wealth is dangerous-when-misused; it is saying wealth marks divine favor. Luke is not saying wealth is fine-when-used-well; he is saying woe to the rich, period.

Walter Brueggemann has argued in The Prophetic Imagination and elsewhere that the canon preserves a sustained internal debate between royal-establishment theology (which sanctifies prosperity) and prophetic-apocalyptic theology (which condemns it). The contradiction is not a misreading by skeptics — it is the actual theological tension that produced the canon. Verdict: real, unharmonizable at face value, and arguably the most important social-theological contradiction in the Bible.

entries.question: Should we rejoice when our enemies suffer?
entries.summary: Psalm 58:10 has the righteous explicitly rejoicing at vengeance and washing their feet in the blood of the wicked. Proverbs 24:17 just as explicitly prohibits gloating: "do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles." The same Hebrew Bible commands both responses.
entries.commentary:
This contradiction is internal to the Hebrew Bible — Psalms versus Proverbs — and it surfaces a real ethical tension that the canon never resolves. Psalm 58 is one of the imprecatory psalms, a category that also includes Psalms 35, 69, 109, and 137. These texts pray for, celebrate, or anticipate violent retribution against enemies. Erich Zenger's A God of Vengeance? remains the standard critical treatment, and Zenger argues — rightly — that these psalms are protest theology from positions of powerlessness, not blueprints for ethics. That is the strongest defense of the imprecatory tradition.

Proverbs 24:17-18 is doing something different. It is moral instruction in the wisdom tradition, advising restraint and warning that Yahweh may transfer his anger from the enemy to the gloater. This anticipates Matthew 5:43-48 ("love your enemies") and Romans 12:17-21 (Paul quoting Proverbs 25:21-22 about heaping coals of fire). The New Testament side of the canon comes down firmly with Proverbs, against the imprecatory psalms.

The apologist harmonization (Wenham, Bonhoeffer's Psalms: The Prayer Book of the Bible, Daniel Estes) treats the imprecatory psalms as prayers leaving vengeance to God rather than personally undertaking it, and reads Psalm 58:10 as eschatological vindication rather than vindictive personal joy. That works for some of the imprecatory psalms but does not really cover Psalm 58:10, where the righteous one personally washes his feet in blood. That is participatory, not merely petitionary. Hossfeld and Zenger's Hermeneia commentary acknowledges the imagery is hard and notes that the psalm assumes a worldview in which divine justice is visible and shared in by the community of the righteous.

The critical-scholarship verdict, articulated most clearly by Walter Brueggemann in Praying the Psalms and David Firth in Surrendering Retribution, is that the imprecatory psalms preserve an ethic the rest of the canon — especially the New Testament — actively rejects. The contradiction is not a surface inconsistency; it is two distinct ethical traditions sitting in the same book. Verdict: real, theologically significant, and the harmonization works only by softening Psalm 58 past its plain sense.

entries.question: Is Salvation by faith alone?
entries.books_in_tension: Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Romans, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, James, 1 Peter, Revelation
entries.summary: Paul stacks Romans 3:28, Romans 4:13, Galatians 2:16, Galatians 3:11-12, and Ephesians 2:8-9 to insist humans are justified by faith apart from works of the law. Then Matthew 19:17 ("keep the commandments"), Matthew 25:31-46 (sheep and goats judged on what they did), Romans 2:6 and 2:13 (Paul himself!), James 2:14-26 ("faith without works is dead"), and Revelation 20:12-13 (judged according to works) all push the opposite direction. This is the Reformation argument compressed into one contradiction page.
entries.commentary:
This is the contradiction that produced Luther's hatred of James ("epistle of straw") and 500 years of Protestant-Catholic dispute. The basic exegetical problem is real and severe. Paul in Romans 3:28 says anthrōpon dikaiousthai pistei chōris ergōn nomou — a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law. James 2:24 says hoti ex ergōn dikaioutai anthrōpos kai ouk ek pisteōs monon — a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. The Greek constructions are direct mirror images. Both use Abraham as the test case. Paul cites Genesis 15:6 to prove Abraham was justified by faith before he did anything; James cites Genesis 22 to prove Abraham was justified by works when he offered Isaac.

The apologist harmonization (Schreiner, Moo, Carson, Blomberg) is the standard New Perspective and Reformed synthesis: Paul opposes works of the law as Jewish boundary markers (circumcision, food laws, Sabbath) used to claim covenant membership; James opposes a dead faith that produces no ethical fruit. On this reading, Paul's "faith" already includes obedient response and James's "works" are the evidence of saving faith. James Dunn, Tom Wright, and Krister Stendahl have refined this into a coherent position, and it does dissolve the contradiction if you grant the lexical premises.

But the harmonization has costs. It requires reading Paul's "works of the law" (erga nomou) more narrowly than the natural Greek allows — Stephen Westerholm and others have argued forcefully that erga nomou means works of the law in general, not just ethnic boundary markers. It also requires reading James's pistis monon (faith alone) as meaning something other than what the words say. Even Romans 2:6-13, in Paul's own letter, contradicts the standard Pauline-faith-alone reading: Paul there says God will judge each person according to their deeds and that the doers of the law will be justified. Paul does not harmonize that with Romans 3 within his own letter.

The critical scholarly position, established since Sanders and refined by Dunn, Wright, and most recently John Barclay's Paul and the Gift, is that the New Testament contains multiple soteriologies that do not flatten into Reformation faith-alone-ism without distortion. Matthew, James, and Revelation operate with a judgment-by-works framework that Paul's polemic against Jewish boundary markers in Galatians and Romans cannot simply override. Verdict: contradiction is real, harmonization is theologically possible but requires importing categorical distinctions the texts do not themselves spell out.

entries.question: Will the righteous flourish?
entries.summary: Psalm 92:12 promises the righteous will flourish like the palm and grow like a cedar of Lebanon. Isaiah 57:1 mournfully observes that the righteous perish, and no one takes it to heart. Same canon, opposite empirical claim.
entries.commentary:
This is the same act-consequence-versus-protest-theology tension we get in the wicked-live-long contradiction (Job 21 versus Proverbs 10), just from the inverse angle. The retribution-principle psalms — and Psalm 92 is a textbook example of confident retribution theology — assert that righteousness produces visible, this-worldly flourishing. The cedar and the palm are images of stability and longevity.

Isaiah 57:1 is in a completely different register. It belongs to what scholars call Third Isaiah (Isaiah 56-66), the post-exilic prophetic material that grapples with the gap between the promises of Second Isaiah and the disappointing reality of the restored community. Joseph Blenkinsopp's Anchor Bible commentary on Isaiah 56-66 reads 57:1-2 as a lament that the righteous die early and no one notices — a direct empirical refutation of the retribution principle that Psalm 92 takes for granted.

The apologist harmonization (Motyer, Oswalt) typically reads Isaiah 57:1 eschatologically — the righteous "flourish" ultimately in the world to come, even when they perish in this one. Psalm 92 is then read as describing the ultimate vindication rather than guaranteed earthly prosperity. This works as theology and is essentially the position the later rabbinic and Christian traditions both adopted. The Hebrew Bible itself, however, does not have a developed concept of personal afterlife reward until late texts like Daniel 12, so reading eschatological consolation back into Psalm 92 is anachronistic. The psalmist meant what he said: the righteous flourish like cedars, in this life.

Walter Brueggemann's typology in The Message of the Psalms distinguishes psalms of orientation (retribution confidence), disorientation (protest, lament), and new orientation (vindication despite suffering). Psalm 92 is firmly orientation; Isaiah 57:1 is disorientation. Both are canonical. Both reflect real Israelite theological positions. They are not the same claim in different words.

Verdict: real contradiction between retribution theology and protest/realist theology, and the harmonization works only by importing an eschatology Psalm 92 doesn't have.

entries.question: Does God sleep?
entries.summary: Psalm 121:3-4 flatly declares that the keeper of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep — a doctrinal claim about Yahweh's perpetual vigilance. Psalm 44:23 just as flatly cries "Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord?" The Psalter contains its own self-refutation on whether God sleeps.
entries.commentary:
This is partly a genre issue and partly a real theological tension. Psalm 121 is a doctrinal psalm — a song of ascents affirming theological propositions about Yahweh's protective character. Psalm 44 is a communal lament responding to military disaster, in which the community accuses God of sleeping through their suffering. The lament genre permits theologically aggressive language that the affirmation-psalm doesn't.

The apologist harmonization is to read Psalm 44:23 as rhetorical and Psalm 121:3-4 as ontological — the lamenter knows God doesn't literally sleep, he is using poetic protest language to provoke divine action. This is essentially right and matches what every commentator from Hossfeld and Zenger to Walter Brueggemann to Mitchell Dahood reads in the Psalter's lament tradition. Goldingay's Psalms commentary makes the same point. The contradiction at the surface level can be eased by recognizing genre.

But there is a real residual tension worth flagging. The Hebrew verb for sleep (yashen) — one of the two terms negated of Yahweh in Psalm 121:4 — appears in 1 Kings 18:27, where Elijah mocks the prophets of Baal by suggesting Baal is asleep — clearly intended as a polemic against a god who can be napped on. The Hebrew Bible's authors knew that a sleeping god was a contemptible god. The fact that Psalm 44:23 can ask Yahweh to wake up suggests that the worldview of that psalm did not absolutize the never-sleeps doctrine the way Psalm 121 does. Mark Smith and Frank Cross have both argued that early Israelite religion was more comfortable with anthropomorphic divine limitations than later monotheistic systematization permitted.

The contradiction here is therefore real but soft: lament-language assumes God can be perceived as sleeping (or actually sleeping in some early-Israelite frameworks), while doctrinal-language insists he never does. The canon preserves both. The harmonization works at the level of "these are different speech acts," which is fair, but it concedes that the texts are saying different things — they are not equivalent claims.

Verdict: surface contradiction, harmonizable through genre analysis, but with theological residue showing how Israelite religion's earlier comfort with limited divine agency got smoothed over in later doctrinal psalms.

entries.question: Can only God work wonders?
entries.summary: Psalm 136:4 praises Yahweh as the one who alone does great wonders (l'oseh nifla'ot gedolot levaddo). 2 Thessalonians 2:9 says the lawless one comes "according to the working of Satan with all power and signs and lying wonders" — terata, the same word used for divine wonders in the Septuagint. If Satan can do wonders, then Yahweh does not do them alone.
entries.commentary:
The contradiction is partly a question of vocabulary and partly a question of cosmology. The Greek of 2 Thessalonians 2:9 uses dynamis (power), sēmeia (signs), and terata (wonders) — pseudous, lying, modifies all three. Apologists (Wanamaker in the NIGTC, Bruce in WBC) standardly read "lying wonders" as either fake wonders that appear real but aren't, or genuine displays of power that mislead viewers about their source. The former reading neutralizes the contradiction: if Satan's wonders are fake, then only God does real wonders.

That reading doesn't quite work though. 2 Thessalonians 2:9 parallels Revelation 13:13-14 (the beast does "great signs, even making fire come down from heaven") and Exodus 7-8 (the Egyptian magicians replicate Aaron's serpent and the first two plagues). In all three cases the text presents the opposing wonders as actually occurring — fire really comes down, serpents really appear from staffs — but with deceptive theological framing. The pseudous in 2 Thessalonians 2:9 most naturally modifies the purpose of the wonders (to deceive) rather than their reality. Charles Wanamaker, Abraham Malherbe in the Anchor Bible commentary, and most critical interpreters take this position.

More importantly, the Hebrew Bible itself already contradicts the Psalm 136 claim. Exodus 7:11-12 has the magicians of Pharaoh duplicating Aaron's wonder, and Deuteronomy 13:1-3 explicitly warns against prophets and dreamers who perform signs and wonders that come true but lead Israel astray — the text assumes such people exist and can perform real signs. The Psalm 136 "alone does wonders" is doxological language affirming Yahweh's uniqueness, not a metaphysical claim that no other agent can produce supernatural phenomena.

The apologist response ("only God does the wonders that count, only God's wonders are salvific") is essentially correct as a theological reading but is itself a harmonization. The Psalm says alone. Other texts disagree. The harmonization works by adding qualifiers — only salvific wonders, only authentic wonders, only ultimately-attributable wonders — that the Psalmist doesn't supply.

Verdict: real surface contradiction; the Hebrew Bible's own narrative texts already complicate the levaddo claim of Psalm 136, before we even get to 2 Thessalonians.

entries.question: Is anyone justified?
entries.summary: Matthew 12:37 has Jesus telling his hearers that by their words they will be justified — implying some are. Psalm 143:2 has the psalmist praying "do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no one living is righteous before you" (in some translations, "justified"). Paul cites this same psalm at Romans 3:20 to argue universal unrighteousness. The contradiction is whether human justification before God is achievable or categorically impossible.
entries.commentary:
The Greek dikaioō and the Hebrew tsadaq family both cover "justify, vindicate, declare righteous." Psalm 143:2 uses lo' yitsdaq lefaneykha kol-hai — "no living being is righteous before you." The psalmist is petitioning Yahweh to suspend strict judgment because no one would pass it. Matthew 12:37 uses the future passive dikaiōthēsē — "you will be justified" — implying the possibility.

The apologist harmonization is the standard imputed-righteousness or two-aspects-of-justification move. Psalm 143:2 establishes that no one is intrinsically righteous; Matthew 12:37 describes a forensic verdict made possible by Christ's atonement or by genuine repentance. R. T. France, Davies and Allison, and Ulrich Luz all read Matthew 12:37 in eschatological-judgment context, with words functioning as evidence of the heart's true state. No one is righteous by works; but words spoken from a regenerate heart will be vindicated at judgment.

This harmonization is theologically coherent within a Pauline-Reformation framework but does not match what Matthew 12:37 is doing in its own gospel context. Matthew 12:36-37 says "every careless word people speak — they will give account for it on the day of judgment, for by your words you will be justified and by your words you will be condemned." This is not Pauline imputed-righteousness language. This is judgment-by-deeds (specifically, judgment-by-speech) language, parallel to Matthew 25:31-46 and to the general synoptic emphasis on works as the basis of eschatological reward. Matthew's soteriology, as Ulrich Luz and Dale Allison both argue, operates with a covenantal nomism similar to Second Temple Judaism rather than with Pauline forensic justification.

The Hebrew Bible itself contains both positions. Job 9:2 ("how can a mortal be just before God?"), Ecclesiastes 7:20 ("there is no one on earth who does good and never sins"), and Psalm 143:2 are on one side. Genesis 18:23-25 (Abraham bargaining for the righteous of Sodom — presupposing some exist), Ezekiel 18 (anyone who turns from wickedness and does righteousness shall live), and the wisdom literature's repeated celebration of the tsaddiq (the righteous person) are on the other.

Verdict: real contradiction between two strands of biblical soteriology. The harmonization through imputed righteousness works as systematic theology but is not what Matthew is actually doing in 12:37.

entries.question: Should we think for ourselves?
entries.summary: Proverbs 2:2, Ecclesiastes 7:25, and 1 Thessalonians 5:21 ("test all things") encourage active critical thinking. Proverbs 3:5 ("lean not on your own understanding") and 2 Corinthians 10:5 ("bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ") push the opposite direction — distrust your own reasoning and submit your thoughts. The Bible's epistemology argues with itself.
entries.commentary:
This contradiction is genuinely interesting because it cuts to the heart of what kind of epistemological authority the biblical tradition assumes. Proverbs 2:2 and Ecclesiastes 7:25 belong to the wisdom tradition, which is unembarrassed about commending the use of one's own mind — Qohelet in particular is the most relentlessly first-person reasoner in the Hebrew Bible, applying his heart to know and search out wisdom by direct investigation. 1 Thessalonians 5:21 has Paul telling the Thessalonians panta de dokimazete — test everything — which is straightforward epistemic activism.

Then Proverbs 3:5 — al-tisha'en el-binatekha, do not lean on your own understanding — appears in the same book, two columns over. Michael V. Fox in the Anchor Yale commentary on Proverbs reads 3:5 not as a blanket prohibition on reasoning but as a contrast between self-sufficient autonomy and trust in Yahweh; the proverb assumes you still use your mind, you just don't make it the final arbiter. That is a real exegetical point. And 2 Corinthians 10:5, in context, is about Paul demolishing rhetorical and philosophical arguments raised against the gospel — the "thoughts" Paul wants to capture are specific opposing logismoi from his Corinthian opponents, not human cognition as such. Margaret Thrall's ICC commentary makes this case carefully.

The apologist harmonization, then, is partly correct: the texts encouraging thought and the texts urging submission can be reconciled by noting that the wisdom tradition wants reasoning under the umbrella of trust in Yahweh, and that Pauline submission-of-thought is about specific oppositional arguments. Fair enough.

But the harmonization papers over a real tension. The wisdom tradition assumes the human capacity for genuine inquiry produces reliable results — Qohelet investigates and reaches conclusions, even uncomfortable ones, on his own authority. Pauline and Johannine literature increasingly subordinates reasoning to revelation and apostolic authority, and the Pastoral Epistles (which most critical scholars take as deutero-Pauline) push this further into "sound doctrine" gatekeeping. There is a trajectory across the canon away from open inquiry and toward conformity, even if no single text outright forbids thinking.

Verdict: the surface contradiction is partly harmonizable through context, but the deeper trajectory from wisdom-tradition inquiry to apostolic-authority submission is real and ideologically significant.

entries.question: Does wisdom make people happy?
entries.summary: Proverbs 3:13 says happy (ashre) is the one who finds wisdom and gains understanding. Ecclesiastes 1:18 says in much wisdom is much grief, and increasing knowledge increases sorrow. Two books of the same wisdom canon, opposite conclusions about whether the pursuit of wisdom delivers happiness.
entries.commentary:
This is a textbook case of an internal canonical debate that critical scholars have been treating as such since at least Crenshaw's early work on the wisdom literature. Proverbs operates on the act-consequence connection — pursue wisdom, gain happiness, long life, and prosperity. The vocabulary throughout Proverbs 3 stacks blessings on the wisdom-seeker: long life, riches, peace, pleasant ways. Michael Fox's Anchor Yale commentary on Proverbs reads chapter 3 as among the most confident expressions of optimistic wisdom theology in the canon.

Ecclesiastes is what happens when a wisdom teacher applies the Proverbs methodology rigorously and discovers that wisdom does not, in fact, deliver happiness. Qohelet's first major experiment in chapter 1 concludes that greater wisdom produces greater awareness of futility — hevel, the famous vapor/breath/absurdity that organizes the whole book. Choon-Leong Seow in the Anchor Bible volume reads 1:18 as Qohelet's deliberate counter to the Proverbs-style optimism. James Crenshaw's commentary makes the same point: Ecclesiastes is wisdom literature interrogating itself.

The apologist harmonization (Estes, Kidner) typically distinguishes between worldly wisdom (which can lead to grief, as Qohelet shows) and the fear-of-Yahweh wisdom (which leads to happiness, as Proverbs claims). Some apologists try to read Ecclesiastes 12:13 (the closing call to fear God and keep his commandments) as the editorial frame that resolves Qohelet's pessimism into Proverbs-style optimism. Tremper Longman's NICOT commentary on Ecclesiastes is reasonably honest about how forced this is — the epilogue does not really overrule the body of the book.

Critical scholarship since Crenshaw, Murphy, and Seow has read Ecclesiastes as deliberate dissent within the wisdom tradition. Qohelet is not contradicting Proverbs by accident; he is contradicting Proverbs on purpose, because his own honest investigation of life produced different results. The canon preserves both voices without harmonization. This is the same internal-debate phenomenon we see in Job versus Proverbs and in the Psalter's mix of orientation and disorientation.

Verdict: real, deliberate contradiction within the wisdom canon. Apologists who try to harmonize the two are forcing one onto the other against the books' own theological projects.

entries.question: Does the bible condemn gambling?
entries.summary: Proverbs 23:4 ("labor not to be rich") is offered as a condemnation of get-rich-quick schemes including gambling. The opposite side stacks Numbers 26:52-56, 33:54, 34:13, and Joshua 14:2, 18:6, 19:51, 21:8 — Yahweh repeatedly commands the land of Canaan to be divided by lot (goral), and Joshua casts lots as a method of divine guidance. If casting lots is gambling, the Bible commands gambling.
entries.commentary:
This contradiction is structurally weak and the SAB framing is over-reaching. Proverbs 23:4 says al-tiga' le-ha'ashir — "do not weary yourself to become rich" — and is part of a wisdom-tradition warning against pursuing wealth as an end. It does not name gambling, and applying it as a gambling-condemnation requires the interpreter to add the specific activity the text never mentions. The SAB is using a generic anti-wealth saying as a prooftext for a specific modern category.

The casting-of-lots side is on firmer ground but still not quite what gambling means in modern usage. Goral in the Hebrew Bible is a divinatory instrument, not a wager. Numbers 26 and Joshua 14-21 use lots to determine tribal land allotments because the procedure was understood to reveal Yahweh's will — Proverbs 16:33 makes the theological framework explicit: "the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD." Acts 1:26 has the early Christians casting lots to select Matthias as the replacement apostle, again as a method of seeking divine guidance, not as a game of chance for monetary gain. Jacob Milgrom's JPS Numbers commentary and Richard Nelson's Joshua commentary both treat lot-casting as a divinatory ritual.

So the SAB has constructed a false contradiction by misidentifying the categories. Proverbs 23:4 is not about gambling. Casting lots in Numbers and Joshua is not gambling in the modern sense — it is sortition for divinely-guided decision-making. There is a genuine biblical lacuna on gambling (the modern category did not exist), and one can argue that wisdom-literature warnings against wealth-pursuit and against laziness do not produce a coherent biblical position on gambling either way.

However, there is a real adjacent contradiction worth noting: the soldiers casting lots for Jesus' garments at the crucifixion (Matthew 27:35, Mark 15:24, Luke 23:34, John 19:23-24, fulfilling Psalm 22:18) is presented as a wicked Roman act, while the same procedure in Numbers and Joshua is presented as divinely commanded. The act of casting lots changes moral valence based on context, which suggests the Bible's treatment is not principled but situational.

Verdict: this specific SAB contradiction is built on weak prooftexts (Proverbs 23:4 is not about gambling). The lot-casting practice itself is divinatory rather than wagering. A real contradiction exists in the adjacent question of whether lot-casting is divinely sanctioned or impious — but that is not what the SAB is asking.
